description_full: Logitech International S.A., through its subsidiaries, designs, manufactures, and markets software-enabled hardware solutions that connect people to working, creating, and gaming worldwide. The company offers products for gamers and streamers, including mice, steering wheels, headsets, keyboards, console gaming headsets, microphones, and streaming services; corded and cordless keyboards and keyboard-and-mouse combinations; pointing devices, such as wireless mouse; conference room cameras, such as ConferenceCams; controllers for video conferencing room solutions; webcams, including streaming cameras; tablet accessories that includes tablet keyboards; headsets, including in-ear headphones and premium wireless earbuds; and mobile speakers and PC speakers, as well as portable wireless Bluetooth speakers. It sells its products to retailers, large and small businesses, end consumers, and e-tailers who resell to retailers, value-added resellers, systems integrators, and other distributors. The company sells its products under the Logitech and Logitech G brand names. Logitech International S.A. was incorporated in 1981 and is headquartered in Lausanne, Switzerland.

Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (1/10).
financial_summary: Logitech International S.A. - R is a large-cap technology business with a $14.5B market cap on $4.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years and +9% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 81% against a 10% cost of capital — a 71-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 37%.

The business throws off $976M in free cash flow — roughly 20 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.46× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 40× is fortress-like.

Management returns a meaningful 5.3% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 16% operating margin runs 9pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.68x).

Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-22.7% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 533 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 12% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 21% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 40% and a beta of 1.12, it moves roughly with the market.
About $76.1M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 30% in the 2020 crash, 49% in the 2022 bear market and 79% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 20% below its DCF fair value of $127, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 52%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $103 to $162 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Technology peers: P/E 18.4 vs 27.4, EV/EBITDA 13.3 vs 17.1 and P/FCF 14.9 vs 26.1 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 10% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 6.7% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 6.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 10 covering analysts target $108 on average, 5% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 81% clears the cost of capital of 10.1% by 71pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.91).
It runs a 37% gross margin and converts 20% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.46x.
ROE of 32% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.7x equity multiplier).
It spends 6.5% of revenue on R&D and 2.3% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $1.7B (12% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 9.0, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 2.2% over 3 years, -1.6% over 5 years and 9.1% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 20%).
At current returns, reinvesting 16% of profits supports about 13.2% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -6.7% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.0x, 1.3% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 16, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.2%), and institutions hold 75%.
It returns 5.3% a year to shareholders (3.7% in buybacks and 1.6% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 2.7% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 12 consecutive years, raising it 9.7% a year over the last five.
people: With about 7,300 employees, each generates about $663K of revenue, 1.8x the Technology median, and revenue has grown 4.6% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $134K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $4.7M (7x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
